newsitem.title: USA: Few electricity suppliers file with California.
newsitem.headline: Few electricity suppliers file with California.

text.p: Despite early expectations of big interest from outside suppliers in California's residential retail electricity market, only a handful have registered with the state.
"We have received two applications so far," Doug Long, manager of the CPUC's electric restructuring project, said Tuesday.
These were from the city of Palm Springs, Calif., which plans to aggregate outside power purchases for residents and from Florida-based Friendly Power Co, Long said.
A Vermont-based company called Green Mountain Energy Resources LLC announced it was registering, but as of Tuesday had not contacted the CPUC.
Green Mountain said it planned to reward customers with "EcoCredits" for using less power and helping the environment.

Under rules passed last year, non-utility companies offering electricity to California residential and small business customers, those with loads under 20 kilowatt hours, must register with the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC).

California residents have been warned in local news reports to expect a deluge of marketing efforts along the lines of those pursued by long-distance phone companies following deregulation of that industry.
The CPUC began accepting power supplier applications Tuesday, ahead of the January 1 launch of retail competition.

The CPUC said it expected to receive more applications later in the week, having had several requests for forms to be mailed out. Companies have also been able since last week to download registration materials from the Internet.
Some industry sources attributed the slow start to companies getting bogged down in the details of deregulation.
"They set up all these rules and make it so that people don't know if they want to register or not," said Bobby Campo, head of Portland General Electric Co's California marketing office.
Still, he also expected lots more companies to register with the state, noting most "are still trying to get their act together."

Industry sources said few companies are likely to initially target residential customers in California, who are guaranteed a 10 percent rate cut for the next four years if they stay with their existing monopoly utility.
"There won't be a big rush to supply the residential market unless you get people to aggregate," Campo said.

Most power suppliers are seen concentrating on snaring deals to supply multi-site buyers such as the University of California system, chain-like commercial customers like department stores, and emerging municipal aggregators such as Palm Springs.
Customers looking to buy power from outside their current utility must register at the CPUC in November.
Long at the CPUC agreed most suppliers are likely to target the state's big commercial and industrial customers, but said those companies would still be well advised to register at the CPUC.
"Just to be sure, I would recommend they spend the $100," he added.
The CPUC application process requires a non-refundable $100 processing fee.
